Another uniform spoke up. “If we launch a strike before the Argentinians can, we'll be able to keep our borders safe.” A suit from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs cleared his throat. “If I may, Mr. President, sending the military to Paraguay is very dangerous. The Argentinians will not hesitate to declare war on us should they feel threatened by an intervention in Paraguay. Instead- we can merely use the idea of a strike as leverage over them.”

The President leaned back into his chair. If Brazilian troops entered Paraguay, it would be likely that Argentina would escalate it into an all-out war in South America. But what if Argentina wasn't cowed by Brazil's threats? What if they didn't stop at the Paraná? It was a hard decision to make, but for the sake of Brazil...
strings.PAR_OAS.17.a: ...Buenos Aires had to be threatened into place.
strings.PAR_OAS.17.b: ...a pre-emptive strike into Paraguay was in order.
strings.PAR_OAS.18.desc:
The world's eyes were on South America.

In Europe, people watched from their living rooms as a TV reporter from the German broadcaster RRG walked along a line of Argentine artillery batteries, the Paraguayan border visible in the background.

A Japanese film crew trawled the grocery stores in Rio de Janeiro, capturing the long lines out the doors, the hesitation in the faces of those affected by the war scare.

A world away, the White House press secretary tried to corral the crowd of journalists, trying to assure the nation that the executive branch took the situation in South America very seriously.

In Brasília, President {bra_getleader} glowered over a table covered in maps, surveillance photos, and intelligence reports. Military officers swarmed around, relaying the facts as they came in; if Argentina invaded Paraguay, they'd be at the Brazilian border in days. Through confidential diplomatic channels, {bra_getleader} had made his counterpart in Buenos Aires aware - if they crossed into Paraguay, Brazil would have no choice but to launch their own invasion. He held a white knuckle grip on the table. He hoped he wouldn't have to follow through with that promise.

The world held its breath, even as the Palácio was a hive of activity. The grim fantasy of Argentine and Brazilian forces meeting in the field, in the rubble of a smaller nation caught in the crossfire, seemed to edge towards reality. Though the heat rolled on, a ringing cut through the noise. A General held the phone receiver to his ear, and spoke. “Mr. President, they're withdrawing. The Argentines are standing down.”
strings.PAR_OAS.18.a: Paraguay's communist regime will live on, but so will everyone else.
strings.PAR_OAS.19.desc:
About a dozen soldiers occupied the farmer's house - two rooms in all - that stood sunbaked by the dirt road. All around were cotton fields, with the horizon sometimes dotted by similarly basic dwellings of the peasants who had worked them. When news came of the revolution in Asunción, they had spontaneously decided to drown the local landlord in the nearby river. Now the peasants too were gone, displaced by the dual invasions or hiding in the forest.

From deployment at the Brazil-Paraguay border, to the invasion itself, Captain Reyes and his company had found the operation mostly uneventful. In fact, they counted one casualty - the radioman had just come down with an upset stomach. Therefore Reyes found himself struggling with the bulky radio set in the hut's main room.

“HQ, do you read? This is... coordinates are...” Reyes repeated a regular patter into the set over and over, growing irritated at the static. Out the front door, two soldiers smoked and sat on the waist-high sandbags. From the other room where they all slept came idle conversation.

“-Confirmed across Chaco... Enemy at Paraná crossing...” The radio whispered, and Reyes focused close. He handled the dials delicately, trying to find the voice. Familiar words in Brazilian Portuguese came back; “-Lack of actionable intel... Multiple positions in the line... Skirmish...”

Skirmishes across the line? Last Reyes had checked, the communists had gone to ground. As Reyes puzzled over the patchwork message, one of the smoking soldiers cried out.

Reyes turned and saw, past the door frame, past the machine gun emplacement, past the cotton field, a column of tanks rolling out of the horizon, tearing down the dirt road.
strings.PAR_OAS.19.a: Who started the shooting war? The Argentine armour rolled ahead anyway.
strings.PAR_OAS.24.desc:
Be respectful. Be vigilant. Don't make friends. Those were the three principles that were drilled into Private Ángel Ortega during his briefings before his deployment in Asunción. Ortega thought that they should've added a fourth of “learn how to entertain yourself.” His job was to kick pebbles and twiddle his thumbs while patrolling the neighborhood a mile or so from Silvio Pettirossi. The days seemed to melt together- making Ortega wish either for a little bit of action or for the announcement that they finally scraped together enough competent cops for the American peacekeepers to pull out.

It was either Thursday or Friday when a soccer ball rolled out of a field in front of his feet. Ortega turned his head, seeing a gaggle of children that looked somewhere between eight and twelve arguing with each other on whose fault it was that the ball got kicked all the way over there. The bickering slowly died down, and then all the kids were staring down Ortega. He wasn't intimidated by a group of scrawny kids. “You want this back?” He asked in Spanish, pointing down to the ball at his feet. Just silence and staring. Ortega scoffed, and kicked the ball back toward the children. The black and white ball rolled up to their feet, but they didn't collect it. They just kept staring and frowning. Fine. Be like that. Ortega kept walking. He heard more conversation and laughter around the corner. As soon as he turned it, the trio of men on the porch of the corner house stopped laughing, and just stared, just like the children. Ortega scowled right back at them and kept walking, kicking a pebble out of his way as he did so. Nothing he was unfamiliar with.
strings.PAR_OAS.25.t: A House of the Americas, Divided
strings.PAR_OAS.25.desc:
As Alfonso García Robles took to his feet, the murmuring of delegates sitting beside and before him in the triangular arrangement of the Hall of the Americas dissipated. As Secretary of External Relations and veteran diplomat, he was familiar with the OAS headquarters in Washington DC, though it was a rare occasion he had reason to address the entire body. But the invasion of Paraguay was one such occasion.

“My fellow delegates, allow me to make clear the Republic of Mexico's opinion.” García Robles spoke directly. “We wholeheartedly condemn the planned invasion of Paraguay. We underst-”

Some of the other delegates jeered. “We understand the Argentinian and Brazilian position, and understand the danger a Communist regime in Asunción poses. None of us are happy to see that poor nation swing from one extreme to another. But such an aggressive response will kill and immiserate thousands of innocents! It will create a generation of martyrs! We must instead respect Paraguay's national sovereignty and open immediate dialogue with the new regime to offer a path of moderation.”

“Rubbish,” said Araújo Castro, the Brazilian representative at the table opposite. García Robles turned to him directly, but his look was almost pitying.

“My good friend, it hurts to hear you say that, when we got along so well during my tenure as ambassador to your great nation. I know the Brazilians as a people of peace! We can spare this beautiful continent another bloody stain, if you only change your mind!”

The room exploded into cross-talk and invective. The Cuban representative cheered and applauded. The Argentine and Brazilian delegates began an angry denunciation. The American chairman simply looked out the window, plainly irritated.
strings.PAR_OAS.25.a: A vote against militarism, cast in defiance of the tide.
strings.PAR_OAS.26.desc:
Hugo B. Margáin's eyes flitted impatiently from the tarmac out of the window to the radio telephone beside him in the cabin of the Washington-bound plane languishing on the airport runway. The early morning light was just cresting the terminal, and the Secretary of External Relations took another swig of coffee. President Salinas would surely call any minute, but the clock was ticking. He needed to be in the air in half an hour if he was to make it to the OAS emergency summit.

Margáin had gone straight to Salinas as soon as it was called, and both men had spent much of the previous night discussing the surprising news - the Americans had successfully brokered a deal between the antagonistic Argentine and Brazilian governments to coordinate, under OAS purview, an invasion of Paraguay to topple the new Communist regime. A resolution for the operation, for procedure's sake, would be put to a vote for all OAS member states, and Margáin cursed the awkward position that put Mexico in.

The debate on how to vote had gone through the night, the arguments hashed over - a vote against on the basis of the Estrada Doctrine's non-intervention would anger Yankee-friendly business leaders and major potential trade partners in Latin America. Margáin would personally suffer, risking contacts and even friendships in the States. Still, he preferred that to a meek abstention, which would be unpopular at home and with the rest of the Veracruz pact - another betrayal of revolutionary ideals from Salinas' government, they would say. It was the kind of bad press they should avoid.

The President, still uncertain, planned to consult Alemán, Barrios, and the others before making a final decision - a decision Margáin restlessly waited for, that morning on the tarmac.
strings.PAR_OAS.26.a: When the call came through, Salinas told him to abstain.
strings.PAR_OAS.26.b: When the call came through, Salinas told him to vote against the resolution.
strings.PAR_OAS.27.desc:
“Can you believe it, Your Excellency?” Antonio Carrillo Flores' voice crackled from the receiver. “Brazil and Argentina have finally found something they agree on.”

Ordaz tapped his desk, and only gave his External Relations Secretary an affirmative hum in reply. Carrillo filled the silence again, calling from a secure line direct from the Mexican Embassy in Washington.

“It's a shame their common ground is invading Paraguay, but they can't be expected to take a gang of Communist guerillas for neighbours. Our friends up here are ecstatic that they brokered the deal, so the whole operation is under OAS auspices. The OAS member states still need to vote for it tomorrow, of course.”

“It's rather like a christening, isn't it?” Ordaz finally and morosely responded. “I assume your present company is leaning on us to vote in favor?”

“They'd prefer that, yes, though at least some of them have heard of the Estrada Doctrine and understand our delicate position. A quiet, no-fuss abstention at the House of the Americas shouldn't rustle too many feathers here or at home.”

Despite the Secretary's words, the thought had been percolating in Ordaz' head - that a vote in favor of the operation would make it clear Mexico didn't brook extremism, and may well work to curry goodwill with the Americans. But the words stuck in his mouth. Questions of foreign policy tended to sit uneasy with him, especially since that humiliating Aleutians episode. The leftists would protest - the Cubans too - he could only expect some angry phone calls from Havana.

“Your Excellency? Is there something wrong with the line? I didn't hear you.”
strings.PAR_OAS.27.a: “Of course, you're right. Make it clear Mexico abstains.”
strings.PAR_OAS.27.b: “Actually Carrillo, we will be voting in favor of the resolution.”
